newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal's disparate coalition faces bumpy road.
newsitem.headline: Nepal's disparate coalition faces bumpy road.

text.p: A party once close to Nepal's monarchy has joined hands with communists in a coalition fraught with contradictions and facing an uncertain future.

A splinter faction of the centre-right Rastriya Prajatantra Party (RPP) and the communist Unified Marxist-Leninist (UML) party were set on Tuesday to take power with a third ally in the Himalayan kingdom.
The coalition is the third ruling combination since general elections in 1994 yielded a badly split parliament with no party holding a clear-cut majority.
The communists led a minority government for 10 months after the elections until their opponents toppled it in September 1995 with a no-confidence motion.
The centrist Nepali Congress then joined hands with the RPP and the smaller Nepal Sadbhavana Party (NSP) in a fractious coalition which ruled until the RPP faction withdrew last week.
Now the tight parliamentary arithmetic has thrown together the breakaway RPP group and its erstwhile foes, the UML.

The RPP consists of leaders from the party-less system which lasted from 1961 to 1990 and was dominated by King Birendra. Under that system, the monarch enjoyed absolute power to select and dismiss prime ministers at will.
UML activists shed blood in pro-democracy demonstrations which forced the king to abandon his absolute powers in 1990.
"Politics makes for strange bedfellows," said Sridhar Khatri, a political science professor at Tribhuvan University in the capital Kathmandu.
Dissident RPP faction leader Lokendra Bahadur Chand, who twice served as prime minister under the former system of no parties, was set to be sworn in as prime minister on Wednesday, officials said.
But as soon as King Birendra tapped Chand on Monday, the durability of the unlikely coalition was questioned.
"His (Chand's) third accession to the prime minister's office has been very swift -- but holds all the promises to be bumpy," the Kathmandu Post newspaper said on Tuesday.
Chand's authority appears shaky due to his faction's sparse representation in the 205-seat lower house of parliament, where he controls a mere 10 votes compared to the UML's 90.
RPP officials said Chand's party was expected to take four cabinet portfolios for every six for the UML.
"It is a government by the UML through the back door," Khatri said.
Another RPP faction led by the party's president, Surya Bahadur Thapa, and which holds nine seats in parliament, did not support Chand. The UML itself was split over whether to support Chand.
Constitutional scholars said the obvious alternative to revolving coalitions -- dissolving parliament and calling snap elections -- was made difficult by a Supreme Court decision in August 1995.
The court overturned a recommendation by then-prime minister Man Mohan Adhikary of the communists to dissolve parliament and call mid-term elections.
The court ruled that dissolution was not allowed if a new government could be formed from the existing parliament.
Analysts said the judgement stripped the prime minister of a weapon that could be used to keep supporters in line.

Constitutional lawyer Ganesh Raj Sharma told Reuters that outgoing prime minister Sher Bahadur Deuba of the Nepali Congress party was unable to threaten rebel lawmakers "because his long stick had been snatched away by the Supreme Court".
"Chand could also meet the same fate as Deuba because of this," Sharma said. "I am afraid of the same fate for Chand."
